title: Complex conjugates and division
keyIdea: The conjugate of z = a + bi is z* = a − bi: keep the real part, flip the sign of the imaginary part. On an Argand diagram z* is the reflection of z in the real axis. z + z* = 2a is real, z − z* = 2bi, and zz* = a² + b² = |z|² is real and never negative. To divide by c + di, multiply the top and bottom by its conjugate c − di, so the denominator becomes the real number c² + d². In modulus–argument terms, dividing divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.
familyTip: Ask your teenager to explain why multiplying by the conjugate 'clears' the i from a denominator, using (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b². Then pick two small complex numbers, have them divide one by the other by hand, and check the answer by multiplying it back.

visual.caption: Real or not real? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: mirror z to get z*, find z from z + z* and z − z*, hunt zz* = 25, realise a denominator, and divide on the Argand diagram.

kid: The conjugate of z = a + bi is z* = a − bi. Keep the real part and flip the sign of the imaginary part. The conjugate of 3 + 4i is 3 − 4i, not −3 − 4i. On an Argand diagram, z* is z reflected in the real axis.
Add them and the imaginary parts cancel: z + z* = 2a, a real number. Subtract them and the real parts cancel: z − z* = 2bi. So if you know both, you can find z.
Multiply them: (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² − b²i² = a² + b². Since i² = −1, the answer is real and equals |z|². So (3 + 4i)(3 − 4i) = 25.

To divide, multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom. For (5 + 5i) ÷ (1 + 2i), use 1 − 2i: the bottom becomes 1 + 4 = 5 and the top becomes 15 − 5i, so the answer is 3 − i. Check by multiplying back: (3 − i)(1 + 2i) = 5 + 5i.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. This is A level Further Mathematics Core Pure (Edexcel 9FM0 2.1 to 2.3, AQA 7367 B, OCR Y540 1.04): find the conjugate, use zz* = |z|², divide complex numbers, and know that |z ÷ w| = |z| ÷ |w| and arg(z ÷ w) = arg z − arg w. Key words: conjugate, modulus, argument, Argand diagram, realising the denominator.

The method mirrors rationalising a surd denominator. Multiplying by c − di is multiplying by 1 in disguise, (c − di) ÷ (c − di), and it turns the denominator into c² + d². The result is (a + bi) ÷ (c + di) = [(ac + bd) + (bc − ad)i] ÷ (c² + d²). Conjugates also explain why real-coefficient polynomials have complex roots in conjugate pairs, and why z + z* and zz* are the sum and product used to rebuild a quadratic from one complex root.

Common mistakes: writing the conjugate as −a − bi or −a + bi; losing the sign through i² so that zz* comes out as a² − b²; multiplying by the conjugate of the numerator, or by the denominator itself; multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate; forgetting to divide both parts by the new real denominator; and adding the arguments when dividing. A quick check is to multiply the answer back by the divisor.

In the lab your student drags z and watches z* mirror it, uses z + z* = 6 and z − z* = 4i to pin down z = 3 + 2i, finds three lattice points with zz* = 25 on the circle |z| = 5, divides (5 + 5i) by (1 + 2i) in four checked steps, then drags w until (2 + 4i) ÷ w = i while the modulus ratio and the argument difference are shown live.

practice.hint: zz* = (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b², because i² = −1.
practice.explain: zz* = {a}² + {b}² = {=a*a+b*b}. It is real and equals |z|².

practice.prompt: z + z* = {a} and z − z* = {b}i, where z = x + yi. What is x + y?

practice.hint: Keep the real part; flip only the sign of the imaginary part.
practice.explain: (−2 + 5i)* = −2 − 5i. The real part −2 stays the same.

practice.prompt: To work out (3 + i) ÷ (4 − 3i), multiply top and bottom by…
practice.hint: Use the conjugate of the denominator.
practice.explain: The conjugate of 4 − 3i is 4 + 3i. Then the denominator becomes 16 + 9 = 25.

practice.hint: Multiply top and bottom by 2 + i. The denominator becomes 5.
practice.explain: (10 + 5i)(2 + i) = 20 + 10i + 10i + 5i² = 15 + 20i, and dividing by 5 gives 3 + 4i. Check: (3 + 4i)(2 − i) = 10 + 5i.

pool.prompt: Where is z* on an Argand diagram?
choices: The reflection of z in the real axis
The reflection of z in the imaginary axis
pool.hint: Only the sign of the imaginary part changes.
pool.explain: z* = a − bi has the same real part and the opposite imaginary part, so it is the mirror image in the real axis.

pool.prompt: Which of these is always real for every complex z?
pool.explain: zz* = a² + b², which is real. z − z* = 2bi is imaginary, and z² is usually complex.

pool.hint: Expand all four terms, then use i² = −1 on the last one.
pool.explain: 4 − 6i + 6i − 9i² = 4 + 9 = 13. Getting −5 means i² was taken as +1.

pool.hint: Multiply top and bottom by 1 − i; the denominator becomes 2.

pool.prompt: arg z = 2π/3 and arg w = π/6. What is arg(z ÷ w)?
w = {a} − {b}i. What is the real denominator after multiplying (1 + i) ÷ w top and bottom by w*?
pool.hint: Multiply w by its conjugate: (a − bi)(a + bi) = a² + b².

pool.prompt: z = {a} + {b}i. What is the real part of z + z*?
pool.hint: The imaginary parts cancel; the real parts double.

pool.prompt: A student writes 1 ÷ i = i. What is the correct value?
pool.hint: Multiply top and bottom by −i, the conjugate of i.
